messages.content: A test suite that calls a sandboxed execution function directly, in-process, reports that containment works correctly. Should that be trusted as proof the real deployed execution path is safe?

No, not by itself. A direct in-process function call bypasses every layer that only exists on the real execution path: process boundaries, path admission checks, command-parsing and argument-matching logic, and any binding of runtime parameters (such as which root directory a sandbox is scoped to) that only gets resolved when the real invocation path runs end to end. In a real instance of this situation, a series of attempts to run a preregistered evaluation through its real execution path surfaced three distinct platform defects that a dry-run-style direct call would never have exercised: a relative script path that failed an admission check, the platform's own terminal layer wrapping an exact command in a multi-line shell script before an already-landed admitted-runner's exact-command matcher ever saw it, and that same admitted-runner binding the whole evaluation root instead of the intended per-run scratch directory, which broadened its write scope and made a downstream containment check fail to match. None of these would show up in a test that invokes the underlying function directly instead of going through the real command-dispatch and admission machinery. The correct practice is to test containment, admission, and execution-path correctness through the actual invocation path a real run will use, not through a shortcut that only proves the underlying logic is correct in isolation.

messages.content: A long-running job is killed for exceeding its time budget. The team raises the budget and it is killed again, just past the new, larger budget. What should this pattern make you suspect, and what should it not make you suspect?

When a job is killed just past whatever time budget is currently configured, repeatedly, across multiple different budget values, that pattern itself is evidence of a hang or a deadlock in the job's own execution path, not evidence that the job is simply slow and needs more time. A job that is merely slow does not reliably die within a small margin of an arbitrary, changing ceiling every time the ceiling changes; a job stuck on a deadlock does exactly that, because it never progresses past the point where it hangs regardless of how much additional wall-clock budget it is given, and the ceiling is the only thing that eventually stops it. In a real instance of this situation, a job was killed just past three different configured wall budgets in sequence, and the failure was first misattributed to ordinary host load or the job being under-provisioned for its true cost. It was later found to be a genuine deadlock: a multiprocessing queue's consumer side was checking whether the producer process was still alive before it had fully drained a large result payload from the queue, so a sufficiently large result could never be read back before any wall-time ceiling, however generous, eventually fired. The lesson is to treat overruns that track the configured limit, whatever that limit currently is, as a signal to look for a hang or deadlock in the execution path first, rather than assuming the workload is simply expensive and needs a bigger number.

messages.content: A short timing probe that exercises a real execution path but returns a small payload finds no problem. A much longer real run through the same path, returning a large payload, then hangs. Does the passing short probe mean the execution path itself is not the problem?

Not necessarily, and it is a mistake to treat a passing short-payload probe as clearing the execution path in general. Some defects, such as a deadlock in how a result is handed back across a process or thread boundary, are triggered specifically by payload size, not by elapsed time: a small result may be written to and read from an inter-process channel fast enough, or in few enough steps, that a race between a liveness check and a drain operation never actually manifests, while a large result crossing the same channel takes long enough, or enough chunks, for that same race to resolve the wrong way. In a real instance of this situation, a deadlock was traced to a multiprocessing queue's consumer performing a liveness check before the queue had been fully drained; short timing probes with small return payloads never exposed it, because the race window they created was too small to matter, while a real, larger production-shaped run that returned a substantially larger payload hit it reliably. The correct inference is that a short, small-payload probe passing tells you comparatively little about payload-size-dependent failure modes on the same execution path; validating the path requires a probe whose payload shape resembles the real workload's, not just one that resembles its rough timing.

messages.content: A sandboxed execution system only allows commands that exactly match an admitted, reviewed command. Someone submits a command that is logically equivalent to the admitted one but is formatted slightly differently -- for example, wrapped across multiple lines, or using a relative rather than absolute path. Should the system run it?

No, and the fact that it might not run is not a bug to work around, it is the containment model working as designed; the correct fix is to submit an exact match, not to relax the matcher. Exact-command admission exists specifically so that what gets reviewed and gated is provably the same thing that executes, with no room for a semantically-equivalent-but-differently-formatted command to slip past review; if the matcher accepted logical equivalents, an attacker or an honest mistake could submit a command that means something subtly different from what was actually approved. In a real instance of this situation, a relative script path failed an admission check that required an absolute path, and separately, an underlying terminal layer wrapped an already-admitted single-line command into a multi-line shell script before an admitted-runner's exact-string matcher ever saw it, so the matcher rejected it every time. In both cases the correct response was to change how the execution reached the matcher -- an exact absolute path, and a command shape the matcher would actually see unwrapped -- not to loosen the admission or matching logic to tolerate the variation. Execution briefs that will be checked against an admitted command should be written in the exact literal form that will be matched, not in whatever form is most readable to a human author.

messages.content: A preregistered statistical rule is applied honestly to real data and produces a clean 'no shift' verdict, with a confidence interval that collapses to a single point at zero. Before treating that as a precise, well-powered null result, what should you check first?

Check whether the interval collapsed to a point because the underlying measurements were genuinely precise, or because almost all of the underlying observations were tied at exactly zero for a reason unrelated to the quantity you actually care about -- a floor effect in the measurement instrument itself. A zero-width or degenerate confidence interval ordinarily signals a tightly and confidently estimated effect; it can instead signal that the instrument almost never produced a nonzero reading for either side of the comparison, in which case the interval is uninformatively narrow rather than precisely narrow, and the 'no shift' label, while a mechanically correct application of the preregistered rule, does not mean what a well-powered null result would mean. In a real instance of this situation, a preregistered decision rule correctly and honestly fired a 'no shift of meaningful magnitude' outcome on a decode-level calibration comparison between two models, with a bootstrap confidence interval of exactly [0, 0]. Reading the underlying per-item data showed that 18 of 20 compared items were exact zero-delta ties between the two models, but only 16 of those 18 were ties at a rate of exactly zero -- the other 2 were ties at a shared nonzero rate -- that a scoring classifier used to produce each rate labelled roughly three-quarters of all generated samples as unclassifiable rather than one of the substantive categories it was designed to detect, and that only two of the twenty items had any nonzero difference between the two models at all. The correct practice was to report the preregistered outcome label exactly as it fired, without relabeling it, while also stating plainly, as an equally important fact, that the label's degenerate interval reflects a floor effect and a high unclassifiable rate in the scoring method rather than a precisely measured absence of any real difference -- and to note that this floor effect weakens, rather than strengthens, any downstream reasoning that assumed the measurement had enough resolving power to detect a real effect had one been present.
